prompt: Each product falls into one cell of Bourne's (1957) and Bearden and Etzel's (1982) public-private luxury-necessity matrix. Identify the category type.

cases.text: Touring kayaks used on club excursions are visible to others and owned by only a subset of households, so peers influence both whether to buy one and which brand to pick.
cases.explanation: Public luxuries are visible and exclusive, attracting strong social influence on both product ownership and brand choice.

cases.text: Almost everyone in a northern city owns a winter commuter coat and wears it in public, so reference-group influence focuses primarily on which brand logo is on the sleeve.
cases.explanation: Public necessities are owned by nearly everyone and used in public, so social influence focuses primarily on brand selection.

cases.text: A dual-zone cellar wine refrigerator sits inside the kitchen out of public view. Friends who visit talk about owning one, while the specific brand is chosen mainly on temperature stability.
cases.explanation: Private luxuries are used out of public view, making ownership socially influenced among peers who discuss them while brand choice depends more on functional traits.

cases.text: Unscented laundry detergent sits in the utility closet and is needed by every household, so neighbors exert almost no pressure on either buying detergent or picking a brand.
cases.explanation: Private necessities are neither visible nor exclusive, resulting in weak reference-group pressure on both product and brand selection.

prompt: For each consumer, which kind of reference group is guiding the choice? Sort the cards.

cards.text: Nadia orders the same black folder that everyone in her choir uses for sheet music.
cards.explanation: She already belongs to the choir and interacts with its members regularly, so it is a membership group.

cards.text: A culinary student buys the knife brand used by award-winning chefs he hopes to work beside one day.
cards.explanation: He admires and wishes to emulate that group of chefs, an aspirational group.

cards.text: Lucas leaves his tour-bus lanyard at home in Paris because he does not want observers to misclassify him as a package tourist.
cards.explanation: He avoids a product linked with a dissociative group whose image he rejects.

cards.text: At the family reunion, Amira's cousins all bring the same board game, so she buys it too.
cards.explanation: Her family is a membership group with frequent direct contact.

cards.text: A first-year business student copies the minimalist notebooks carried by senior venture partners she admires.
cards.explanation: She wishes to emulate senior partners, a group she does not currently belong to.

cards.text: Theo stops wearing a jacket style after noticing it has become the signature look of a group whose values he actively rejects.
cards.explanation: He drops the style because it is linked with a dissociative group.

cards.text: Members of a cycling club Jon joined last year all ride with the same helmet, and he buys one.
cards.explanation: He already belongs to and rides with the cycling club.

cards.text: A weekend jogger buys the carbon-plated racing shoes that elite marathoners wear in championship photos.
cards.explanation: Elite marathoners are an idealized aspirational group the jogger wishes to emulate.

prompt: Each consumer is influenced by a reference group. Identify which of Park and Lessig's (1977) three influence mechanisms is operating.

cases.text: Before buying winter tires, Priya consults her uncle, an experienced auto mechanic, about which tread compound grips ice best.
cases.explanation: She accepts information from a knowledgeable source as credible evidence about reality.

cases.text: Sam wears a dark tailored suit to his law firm's client dinner so the senior partners will approve of his professional deportment.
cases.explanation: He conforms to workplace expectations to gain social rewards and avoid sanction.

cases.text: Mia buys a certified zero-waste backpack because using it reinforces her own self-concept as an environmentally committed citizen, even when hiking alone.
cases.explanation: She adopts the group's consumption pattern to enhance her self-concept and express shared values internally.

cases.text: Kenji reads detailed testing threads written by audio engineers on a specialist forum before ordering studio monitors.
cases.explanation: He relies on expert evidence to reduce uncertainty in a technical purchase.

cases.text: In her new department, Rosa switches to the travel mug brand her teammates use after noticing they tease anyone who brings disposable cups.
cases.explanation: She conforms to the peer group's expectations to avoid social disapproval.

cases.text: Omar buys a vintage-style film camera associated with independent art-house filmmakers to express his creative identity.
cases.explanation: He chooses the product to express shared values and identity rather than to comply with external enforcement.

prompt: Match each of French and Raven's (1959) five bases of social power with the marketplace situation that illustrates it.

pairs.match: Fans copy the sunglasses worn by a musician they deeply admire and identify with.
pairs.explanation: Referent power derives from emotional identification and admiration for the source.

pairs.match: A university course syllabus requires students to purchase a specific statistical software license.
pairs.explanation: Legitimate power derives from a socially recognized role, contract, or institutional mandate.

pairs.match: A licensed pharmacist recommends a specific non-drowsy antihistamine based on clinical pharmacology training.
pairs.explanation: Expert power derives from perceived specialized knowledge, training, or access to facts.

pairs.match: A hotel program grants complimentary suite upgrades and bonus points to members who book directly.
pairs.explanation: Reward power derives from the capacity to provide tangible or social benefits.

pairs.match: A homeowners' association levies a monetary fine on residents who install non-approved exterior lighting.
pairs.explanation: Coercive power derives from the capacity to inflict punishment, fines, or social ostracism.

question_text: Jade asks a general-purpose conversational AI assistant which espresso grinder to buy. Within two seconds, it produces a fluent, authoritative comparison table and names a top pick. Why can relying on this response as expert advice be risky?
hint: Compare how a general-purpose language model presents answers across domains with how human specialist credentials work.
correct_answer_citation: Week 10: Attributed Expert Power in Conversational AI Assistants

options.option_text: Because conversational AI assistants never influence which brands enter a consumer's consideration set
options.option_explanation: Attributed expert power grants the AI assistant substantial influence over both the consideration set and the final choice.

options.option_text: Because language models speak hesitantly whenever their underlying product evidence is weak
options.option_explanation: General-purpose AI assistants present uniform linguistic fluency even across domains where their underlying evidence varies widely in quality.

options.option_text: Because the assistant presents uniform fluency across domains, which can cue attributed expert power even when the consumer has not verified the underlying product facts
options.option_explanation: Correct. Instantaneous, fluent synthesis leads users to attribute high expert power and defer to the recommendation without verifying the underlying facts.

options.option_text: Because French and Raven's taxonomy of social power applies only to face-to-face human interactions
options.option_explanation: Consumers attribute expert power to conversational AI assistants in the same way they attribute it to human specialists.

prompt: Each person guides another consumer's purchase. Identify whether the informer is an opinion leader, a market maven, or a surrogate consumer.

cases.text: Friends ask Leo which mirrorless camera lens to buy. He follows optical engineering closely, but has little to say about groceries or apparel.
cases.explanation: Opinion leadership is monomorphic (domain-specific) and rooted in deep involvement in a single product category.

cases.text: Grace tracks store openings, coupon policies, and seasonal price drops across groceries, electronics, and travel, and loves initiating tips with neighbors.
cases.explanation: A market maven possesses broad general marketplace knowledge across many categories and actively shares it.

cases.text: Busy homeowners hire an interior designer to research, select, and purchase all the living-room furniture on their behalf.
cases.explanation: A surrogate consumer is formally retained or delegated to execute search and purchase decisions on the buyer's behalf.

cases.text: In her marathon club, Ana is the runner everyone consults about gps watches and hydration vests, a category she tests every week.
cases.explanation: She is highly involved and knowledgeable in a specific product domain and advises peers within it.

cases.text: A buyer pays an independent auto-buying agent to evaluate inventory, negotiate dealer pricing, and finalize a vehicle lease for him.
cases.explanation: The agent acts as a compensated surrogate consumer formally delegated to make the transaction.

cases.text: Ibrahim keeps track of which supermarkets, hardware stores, and pharmacies across town run the best weekly promotions and tells coworkers every Monday.
cases.explanation: His expertise spans general marketplace practices across many categories rather than one specialized domain.

question_text: A rogue seller uses a generative language model to post hundreds of varied, realistic five-star reviews attributed to fictional customers. How do these synthetic reviews affect the marketplace?
hint: Consider the 'lemons market' problem, the 2024 FTC rule, and who reads online reviews today.
correct_answer_citation: Week 10: Synthetic Reviews, Credibility Erosion, and Regulatory Bans

options.option_text: They are easy for human shoppers to spot immediately because generative AI can only repeat identical template sentences
options.option_explanation: Unlike older template spam, generative language models vary sentence structure and mention specific product attributes, making inspection difficult.

options.option_text: They erode the informational value of all eWOM, violate the 2024 FTC ban on fake reviews, and simultaneously mislead human shoppers and AI shopping agents
options.option_explanation: Correct. Widespread synthetic reviews create a lemons-market collapse in trust, are prohibited under the 2024 FTC final rule, and corrupt both human and AI agent decisions.

options.option_text: They deceive human readers, but autonomous AI shopping agents automatically ignore all customer review text
options.option_explanation: AI shopping agents also ingest customer reviews and review summaries to score candidate products, so synthetic reviews corrupt agent decisions too.

options.option_text: They are permitted under U.S. regulations as long as the text describes real product features accurately
options.option_explanation: The 2024 FTC final rule explicitly prohibits fake consumer reviews, including AI-generated reviews attributed to non-existent individuals.

question_text: A brand manager is considering hiring a computer-generated virtual influencer for an upcoming campaign. Based on consumer research (Lou et al., 2023), in which scenario is the virtual influencer most likely to trigger consumer skepticism?
hint: Think about the authenticity deficit when a digital avatar lacks human sensory and lived experience.
correct_answer_citation: Week 10: Virtual Influencers and Perceived Authenticity

options.option_text: Showcasing a futuristic streetwear silhouette in a clearly labeled digital fashion lookbook
options.option_explanation: Virtual influencers can be effective for symbolic or fashion-oriented campaigns when their artificial nature is transparent.

options.option_text: Announcing a new gaming peripheral in a stylized sci-fi animation
options.option_explanation: Technology-oriented and symbolic campaigns fit a transparent digital character well.

options.option_text: Claiming that a soothing facial moisturizer healed the avatar's dry winter skin over two weeks of daily use
options.option_explanation: Correct. Virtual influencers lack skin and lived sensory experience, so experiential or health claims trigger skepticism and erode brand trust.

options.option_text: Appearing in multiple international ad formats on the same day without travel delays
options.option_explanation: Instant global scalability and creative control are operational advantages of virtual influencers, not sources of sensory skepticism.
